For n-hexadecane pyrolysis at 773K and 10s residence time, simulations captured 11 of 14 experimentally observed olefins within ±5 wt%, including major contributors in the C –C , C –C , and C –C ranges. A second major theoretical contribution addressed unsaturated hydrocarbon degradation, which is critical for mixed plastic streams. Using the Minimum Energy Crossing Point (MECP) method combined with all-electron MP2 calculations, we quantified spin- forbidden C–C homolysis barriers in decene isomers at 773 K, with activation free energies ranging from ~256 kJ/mol at resonance-stabilized sites to >440 kJ/mol adjacent to double bonds. These results establish a quantitative structure–reactivity relationship for unsaturated polymers and explain why unsaturation can either suppress or accelerate degradation depending on the local bonding environment. Other theoretical work in the project focused on a DFT-based analysis of PVC pyrolysis and showed that degradation initiates at tertiary chloride defects and accelerates through conjugation growth and HCl autocatalysis, while large kinetic barriers for aromatic formation (ΔG‡ ≈ 238 kJ/mol) rationalize low aromatic yields (Papanikolaou et al., 2023). Topic Area 4 – Catalytic Upgrading of Plastic Oils into Aromatics and Olefins: Area 4 focused on the catalytic upgrading process of plastic-derived wastes and oils from Area 3, testing heteroatom-free materials over optimized cracking and upgrading catalysts in both fixed-bed and fluidized bed reactors. The project successfully achieved all planned milestones through systematic development of catalyst systems, optimization of regeneration protocols, and demonstration of sustained performance over extended operational periods. Catalyst performance was tested for the cracking, dehydrogenation, and aromatization of heteroatom-free product stream provided by Xianglan Bai and the rest of the topic area 3 team. demonstrating the performance of optimized zeolite catalysts for cracking, dehydrogenation, and aromatization reactions. The research employed systematic acid site engineering to understand and control product selectivity through modification of catalyst surface chemistry. Three distinct catalyst materials were synthesized to investigate the role of acid site distribution in product selectivity. Material 1 (M1) contained aluminum as the sole active site, featuring Al(OH) and Si-OH-Al Brønsted acid sites (878 μmol/g total Al, with 456 μmol/g as SiOHAl sites). Material 2 (M2) maintained identical aluminum and SiOHAl content but incorporated m₂etal-OH (M-OH) species through solid- state incorporation (SSI), replacing AlOH sites with M-OH groups. Material 3 (M3) featured Al(OH) sites with Si-ONa-Al, providing insights into isolated acid site behavior. Model compoun₂d studies using 1-butene (5% in N ) at 475 °C over 10 mg catalyst revealed significant differences in product distribution. The catalysts demonstrated stable performance over 4-hour test periods with less than ₂2% activity loss. At iso-conversion conditions (26% 1-butene cracking conversion), the M2 catalyst exhibited markedly enhanced olefin selectivity with negligible paraffin and aromatic formation compared to M1.
